title: Living with Volcanoes
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: More than thirteen hundred volcanoes on land are considered potentially active, and about fifty of them erupt in an average year. Most lie along the edges of tectonic plates, especially around the Pacific Ocean in a belt known as the Ring of Fire. Where one plate is forced beneath another, rock melts deep in the Earth and rises as magma. Others, such as those of Hawaii, sit over hot spots, where a plume of heat rises from deep in the mantle through the middle of a plate.

A typical volcano consists of a magma chamber, a few kilometres below the surface, from which a conduit leads upwards to a vent. When the pressure in the chamber becomes greater than the strength of the rock above it, magma is forced up the conduit. Once it reaches the surface it is called lava. Over many eruptions, layers of lava and ash build a cone around the vent, and the crater at the top marks the place from which material has been thrown out.

Not all eruptions are alike, and the thickness of the magma decides how violent they are. Runny magma, as in Hawaii, lets gas escape easily, so the lava flows quietly for long distances. Thick, sticky magma traps gas, and the pressure builds until the volcano explodes. The 1980 eruption of Mount St Helens in the United States removed the top four hundred metres of the mountain in a few seconds. The 1815 eruption of Tambora in Indonesia was larger still, and the ash it threw into the atmosphere cooled the planet so much that 1816 became known in Europe as the year without a summer.

Despite the danger, about eight hundred million people live within one hundred kilometres of an active volcano. One reason is that volcanic soil is rich in minerals, and farmers on its slopes can grow several crops a year. Volcanic regions also supply geothermal energy: in Iceland, a large share of the country's electricity comes from this source, and hot water from the ground heats most homes. Tourists add to the income of these places, which makes it even harder to ask the people who live there to leave.

Predicting eruptions is difficult, but scientists have learned to read the warning signs. Before an eruption, rising magma causes many small earthquakes, and the ground may swell by several centimetres. Instruments also measure the gas that escapes from the vent, and a sudden increase in sulphur dioxide often means that magma is close to the surface. Satellites can detect the swelling from space. In 1991, such warnings allowed scientists to persuade tens of thousands of people to leave the area around Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines days before it erupted, and thousands of lives were saved.

However, forecasts are never certain. Some volcanoes show signs for months and then fall quiet, while others give almost no warning at all. Evacuating a city that is then not threatened is expensive, and it may cause people to ignore the next order. Dr Mateo Ruiz, a volcanologist, argues that the best protection is not prediction but preparation: clear evacuation routes, regular drills and honest communication with the public. 'A good plan', he says, 'works even when the forecast is wrong.'

Scientists also study a rarer danger, the supervolcano. Such a volcano can produce an eruption a thousand times larger than that of Mount St Helens. The last one, at Lake Toba in Indonesia, took place about 74,000 years ago, and some researchers think that it reduced the human population to a few thousand. Most experts regard another eruption of that size in the near future as extremely unlikely, but they say it would be a global disaster with effects lasting for years.
